build.title: Beneath the cladding
build.lead: In the drawings, weathered boards meet a black metal roof. A low steel frame sits beneath the house.
build.exterior: We’re planning an air gap behind the cladding so the boards can dry between rain showers. The door and window frames are shown in black.
build.structure: The drawings show two long steel beams joined by shorter crossbeams beneath the floor. Their dimensions are still open.

materials.title: Old timber, new house
materials.lead: We want to give old boards a second life as cladding. Once we find the timber, its material passport will record where it came from and how it was used.

items.name: Malmfuru (heartwood pine)
items.lead: Norwegian builders have long used the reddish-brown heartwood of pine for cladding. We’re looking for old boards cut from slow-grown trees.

items.name: European oak
items.lead: We’re planning oak where a hand rests on a window sill and a foot crosses the threshold.

items.name: Copper
items.lead: In the bathroom concept, a copper edge traces the mirror against deep teal tiles.

items.name: Steel
items.lead: In the drawings, a steel frame ties the base together beneath the house.

living.title: Inside MiniHouse
living.lead: The kitchen and window seat share one room in the drawings. Drawers tuck beneath the seat, with a bathroom at one end of the house.

status.title: Where the project stands
status.body: MiniHouse is still on the drawing board. We’re working on the steel frame and looking for timber for the cladding.

items.q: Does the house need a building permit?
items.a: It depends on how the house will be used, and the municipality decides.
MiniHouse is a house concept still in development. There’s no finished model for sale.

items.q: When will the prototype be ready?
items.a: We don’t have a date for a prototype yet.
The goal is to move it in one piece by truck. Every route has to be checked before it is used.
A concept image shows how we imagine the house. The bathroom images explore colours and materials while its layout is still open.

items.q: Which timber do you hope to reuse?
items.a: We’re looking for old pine boards for the cladding. Once we find a suitable batch, we plan to record where the boards came from and how they were used.

meta.title: MiniHouse: How the idea started
meta.description: How MiniHouse began: from the demolition of an old teachers' residence in Bergen to a small house made to be moved.

story.title: How the idea started
story.lead: I want to revisit a few concepts behind my MiniHouse project, starting with how the idea came to life.
intro: In 2026, I was involved in the demolition of the old Midtun School Teachers' Residence at Øvsttunvegen 21 in Bergen, Norway.

It was a beautiful old building with character, history and memories attached to it. The property was being redeveloped, with a new building planned for the site that would preserve the architectural character and form of the original.
One of the redevelopment project's objectives was to reuse as much of the existing building material as possible.
noticed: Working on that demolition made me look at construction waste differently.
As we dismantled the building, I kept noticing the quality of the old timber. Some pieces had been there for decades, yet they still looked remarkably good and potentially useful.
It seemed such a waste to throw away materials that had already served one generation and could potentially serve another.
That experience made me ask myself a simple question:
story.question: Why should the life of a building's materials end when the building itself is demolished?
story.questionFollow: What if we could take those materials and create something entirely new?

sections.title: From demolition waste to emergency housing
paragraphs: My idea is to design and build small, prefabricated emergency homes, approximately 3 × 6 metres, using reclaimed timber and other reusable construction materials wherever practical and safe.
The houses would be built around a properly engineered structural frame, designed to make them strong enough for transportation and suitable for lifting and relocation by crane.
I want these homes to be practical, comfortable and durable, but also easy to manufacture, transport and deploy.
They could provide temporary accommodation for people affected by emergencies, natural disasters or other situations where safe housing is urgently needed.

sections.title: Giving old materials a new purpose
paragraphs: MiniHouse is not simply about building tiny homes.
It's about bringing together emergency preparedness, engineering, sustainable construction and the circular economy.
I want to show that materials recovered from demolition sites can become valuable resources rather than automatically ending up as waste.
The idea is to preserve what is still useful, combine it with modern engineering and create something that serves a completely new purpose.

Of course, every reclaimed material would need to be assessed for its suitability. Structural safety, insulation, moisture protection and long-term durability would remain essential parts of the design.

sections.title: The bigger vision
paragraphs: My long-term goal is to develop a repeatable system for manufacturing transportable emergency homes, starting with one properly engineered prototype.
If the concept works, MiniHouse could eventually become a practical way to transform suitable demolition materials into safe, sustainable emergency housing.
What began as a thought on a demolition site could become something much bigger.

story.closing: Instead of seeing demolition as the end of a building's story, I want to see it as an opportunity to begin another.

teaser.body: The story behind MiniHouse starts on a demolition site in Bergen, with old timber that was still in good condition.
